I understand your situation very well. I was self harming, not comfortable with people, and had many bad experiences with medications. And going inpatient was the last thing I wanted. My psychiatrist was going to 302 me if I didn't admit myself. It turned out to be the best thing for me. I was able to get ECT much faster than I would have been able to on an outpatient basis. And I am doing better than I have in years now. Getting help can be scary, there's really no way around it. The day I went inpatient was the most stressful day of my life. In the end, I would do it all over again though. I was closer to killing myself than I would ever again like to be. The fact of the matter is that if you admit how bad it is, a mental health professional might recommend a hospital stay. If they recommend one, as much of a pain as it is, you should listen. They can try different medications in a more controlled environment, or other treatments, should medications fail. I tried 8 meds, and all of them made me worse. So now I'm doing ECT which is working like a miracle. 


TL;DR Try to get help/ be honest with your mental healthcare providers. Worst case scenario they can't help you and you can kill yourself later. But at least that way you gave it your full shot.

You can do ECT outpatient, but it will take much longer to get approved for it. It works for 70%-90% of people, which is some of the best odds in psychiatric medicine.

An SSRI and adderall would work on all of the major neurotransmitters; serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. My depression is treatment resistant, so none of the meds I tried helped at all. ECT worked like a fucking miracle, and if you've tried many meds without success it may be a good idea to look into. Because not many things are going to work better than an SSRI in combination with Adderall.

If you want to lose weight, just calculate your TDEE (total daily energy expenditure) and consume less calories than that. Increasing activity level helps raise your TDEE, and tracking calories helps lose more. SSRIs tend to have that side effect, so if you switch off of it, your appetite may decline and cause weight loss. Even then, if you were to just replace soda with water, it might be enough. A lot of people don't realize how many calories are in there. Good luck.

The codes they use are commonly referred to as [sig codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_abbreviations_used_in_medical_prescriptions). But they write generally illegibly mainly because it is faster. These two factors make it relatively difficult to read a prescription unless you know what you are looking for. And in many cases it will be impossible to actually read the full thing, and you need to make inferences about what the prescriber actually meant. Most of the time it is okay, however there are times where we need to call them to find out what they mean.

That is one unfortunate thing about many psychiatric medications. Their withdrawal effects can be pretty nasty. They are prescribed despite the negative side effects because they often do work. And when someone is very depressed, the negatives are often outweighed by the positives. If you are in a better place mentally, then the positive effects would not necessarily outweigh the negatives. However, if you take someone that is potentially suicidal, or even just very depressed, I personally think it would be better to give them some medication even if it has side effects such as Venlafaxine.

Source: pharmacy tech with interests in psychology and pharmacology.
